restatements.text: Repeals the state law requiring cities to allow two homes on single-family lots and gives cities the authority to determine the number of homes allowed on each residential lot.

findings.direction: Shifts authority over residential zoning and density from the state to local governments

analysis.answer: Current law requires cities to allow up to two homes on any single-family zoned lot without a public hearing. The measure repeals this requirement and returns the authority to set the number of homes allowed on residential lots to each individual city.

Many cities will likely revert to stricter single-family zoning rules, making it more difficult and expensive to build additional units on residential lots. Homeowners in those cities will lose the automatic right to build a second unit without going through discretionary local approval processes.

The measure addresses local objections to state preemption of zoning laws by restoring municipal control over housing density. However, this mechanism removes a tool meant to address housing shortages, potentially leading to fewer homes being built and higher entry barriers in cities that choose to restrict density.

City councils, local zoning boards, and local residents who favor stricter development rules gain power and discretion over land use, while state authorities and property owners seeking to build second units lose guaranteed options.

gain.empty_reason: The measure does not advance any of the evaluated concerns, as it removes existing statewide housing allowances.
